title: Practice in the dark
hookLine: a lamp blows out at dinner and Arjuna learns what practice does; abhyasa, and the breath routine built this week
carry: abhyasa is practice that works in the dark
tomorrow: a little girl asks who her groom will be. the answer is a god.
last: THE CONCH IS BREATH OFFERED AS HOLY SOUND.

lines: HIS HAND STILL KNOWS THE WAY.
cards: In the Mahabharata, the young princes are learning archery from their teacher Drona, and Arjuna is the keenest of them all. One night he's eating dinner when a gust of wind blows out the lamp. Total dark.
And Arjuna notices something. His hand still finds his mouth. Every bite.
He doesn't need to see. Years of doing it every day have taught his hand the way.

teach.b: So Arjuna starts practicing archery at night, in the dark. Drona hears a bowstring twanging after everyone's asleep, goes out, finds him, embraces him, and promises to make him an archer without equal.
Later in the same epic, Krishna gives the idea its name.
You heard it on day ninety-eight: Arjuna complains that the mind is as restless as the wind, and Krishna says it can still be held, by abhyasa, practice, and by letting go.
Abhyasa means steady practice, again and again, over a long time.
It's one of Hinduism's most practical teachings: the mind isn't changed in one big moment, but by small repetitions, until it knows the way in the dark.
It's why so many Hindus keep a daily practice: a lamp at the shrine, a few minutes of prayer, a few minutes of breath. This week built yours.
The word for that breath work is pranayama: prana, breath and life, and ayama, lengthening; some read it as yama, restraint.

teach.h: PRANAYAMA: THE FOURTH OF EIGHT STEPS.
teach.b: In the classic picture of yoga it's the fourth of eight steps, after how you treat others, how you live, and how you sit. Here's your five minutes. Watch the breath for thirty seconds.
Four in, six out, for a minute. A soft two-count pause, only if it's comfortable. Five rounds of alternate nostrils.
Three long hums. A minute of ujjayi, then let it fade, and sit.

teach.h: ABHYASA IS PRACTICE THAT WORKS IN THE DARK.
teach.b: On a rushed morning, two pieces is still the practice. What matters is coming back.

how: Many Hindus keep a daily practice (lighting a lamp, a short prayer, japa or a few minutes of pranayama), often in the early morning before meditation or puja; teachers stress abhyasa, steady repetition, over occasional big efforts.

o: lengthening the breath, as a daily practice
holding still in a seated yoga pose

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: where breath practice sits in yoga's eight

s: Arjuna practiced archery at night after the lamp blew out at dinner
his hand found his mouth in the dark, so he trained in the dark too.
in Hindu teaching, the restless mind is changed by one big moment of effort
Krishna says it's held by abhyasa, steady practice over time, and by letting go.
in yoga's eight steps, breath practice comes first
it's fourth: after how you treat others, how you live, and how you sit.

games.q: it's a rushed morning and you have ninety seconds. what fits today's teaching?
o: skip it; if it can't be the full five minutes, it doesn't count.
do two pieces: watch the breath, then four in, six out.
do all six as fast as you can.
games.why: abhyasa is coming back, again and again. two pieces today keeps the hand knowing the way.

practice: Here's the short version, to fit the time: watch three breaths just as they are, then four in, six out, three times, then three rounds of alternate nostrils. One long hum, mmm, and then, mouth closed, a few soft ocean breaths.
Then let it all go and just sit, the way Arjuna's hand found the way without looking.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama. Prana, breath and life; ayama, lengthening. The practice of the breath, the fourth step of yoga.
